Absent
AB-sent
a.
From Latin absens, present participle of abesse, to be away, from ab (from) and esse (to be). Webster 1828: not present; away. Paul uses the word for the believer’s death, and in doing so denies the soul any interval of sleep or unconsciousness.

Biblical Definition

Paul’s statement about dying is short and it settles a great deal: We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Two propositions are joined by nothing but a comma, and the joining is the doctrine — absence from the body is presence with the Lord, with no third condition between them. The chapter has already used the figure of a tent taken down and a house not made with hands, and Philippians 1:23 says the same thing from the other side: to depart and to be with Christ is far better. The word also does ordinary apostolic work. Paul rules on a case in Corinth without being there: I verily, as absent in body, but present in spirit, have judged already (1 Corinthians 5:3) — and the judgment is real church discipline, not sentiment. To the Philippians he ties his absence to their steadfastness: that whether I come and see you, or else be absent, I may hear of your affairs, that ye stand fast in one spirit (Philippians 1:27). A church is what it is when the apostle is not watching.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines ABSENT as not present; not in company; at such a distance as to prevent communication; and figuratively, heedless, inattentive to what is passing.

expand to see more

ABSENT, a. — Not present; not in company; at such a distance as to prevent communication.

Heedless; inattentive to persons present, or to subjects of conversation.

ABSENT, v.t. — To depart to such a distance as to prevent intercourse; to retire or withdraw.

ABSENCE, n. — A state of being at a distance in place; want; destitution.

Latin absens, from ab, from, and sum, esse, to be.

Key Scripture

2 Corinthians 5:8 — "We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord."

1 Corinthians 5:3 — "For I verily, as absent in body, but present in spirit, have judged already, as though I were present, concerning him that hath so done this deed,"

Philippians 1:27 — "Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ: that whether I come and see you, or else be absent, I may hear of your affairs, that ye stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel;"

Colossians 2:5 — "For though I be absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit, joying and beholding your order, and the stedfastness of your faith in Christ."

Modern Corruption

2 Corinthians 5:8 leaves no room for soul sleep, purgatory, or annihilation at death: the believer who is absent from the body is at that moment present with the Lord.

expand to see more

Three errors are excluded by this one verse. Soul sleep — the teaching that the soul is unconscious between death and resurrection, held by the Seventh-day Adventists and the Jehovah’s Witnesses — cannot survive a text in which absence from the body is presence with Christ; an unconscious presence is not what Paul means by far better (Philippians 1:23), nor what our Lord promised the thief for that same day (Luke 23:43). Purgatory is excluded by the same immediacy: if the believer is with the Lord upon dying, there is no penal interval to be shortened by masses or indulgences, and the doctrine that supplies one denies the sufficiency of Christ’s satisfaction. Annihilationism is excluded because the one who is absent from the body still exists to be present with someone. The 1689 Confession states the settled position: the souls of the righteous are received into the highest heavens, and the souls of the wicked cast into hell, and besides these two places Scripture acknowledges none.

A second point belongs here, because the intermediate state is often preached as though it were the whole hope. It is not. Paul’s longing in 2 Corinthians 5 is not to be a disembodied spirit but to be clothed upon — he says explicitly that he does not wish to be found naked. Being with Christ at death is far better; the resurrection of the body is better still, and it is the Christian hope properly so called. Funeral preaching that stops at the soul in heaven has stopped one article short of the creed, which confesses the resurrection of the body and the life everlasting.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek ekdemeo (G1553), to be away from home, to be absent; endemeo (G1736), to be at home, to be present; apeimi (G548), to be away.

expand to see more

Greek ekdemeo (G1553) — to be out of one’s home country, to be absent; absent from the body (2 Corinthians 5:8).

Greek endemeo (G1736) — to be at home, to be present; the deliberate counterpart in the same verse.

Greek apeimi (G548) — to be away; used of Paul’s bodily absence from Corinth and Colosse (1 Corinthians 5:3; Colossians 2:5).

Greek analuo (G360) — to loose anchor, to depart; to depart, and to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23).

Greek skenos (G4636) — a tent or tabernacle, Paul’s figure for the body in 2 Corinthians 5:1.

Usage

"Absent from the body, and... present with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8) — two propositions joined by a comma, with no third state between them."

"Absent in body, but present in spirit, have judged already (1 Corinthians 5:3) — real church discipline exercised at a distance."

"Whether I come and see you, or else be absent... ye stand fast (Philippians 1:27) — a church is what it is unwatched."
